name: Barnum effect
mechanism: vague, generic personality statements feel personally accurate because they're written to apply to almost anyone
example: horoscopes and personality quizzes feel eerily accurate
hook_subject: horoscopes feel like they're describing you exactly
topic: Why do horoscopes feel like they're describing you exactly?

name: Placebo effect
mechanism: believing a treatment will work can trigger real physiological changes, even when the treatment itself does nothing
example: sugar pills can measurably reduce pain in clinical trials
hook_subject: a fake pill can make real pain go away
topic: Why does a fake pill make real pain go away?

name: Nocebo effect
mechanism: expecting a treatment to cause harm can produce real negative symptoms, even from an inactive substance
example: patients told about side effects are far more likely to report them, even on placebo
hook_subject: just reading a list of side effects can make you feel sick
topic: Why does just reading a list of side effects make you feel sick?

name: Framing effect
mechanism: the exact same information leads to different decisions depending on how it's worded, like 90 percent survival versus 10 percent mortality
example: doctors get different patient decisions just by rephrasing identical statistics
hook_subject: the same fact can sound completely different depending on how it's worded
topic: Why does the same fact sound completely different depending on how it's worded?

name: Overconfidence effect
mechanism: people consistently rate their own knowledge and skill higher than it actually is, especially in areas they know only a little about
example: most drivers rate themselves as above average, which is statistically impossible
hook_subject: almost everyone rates their own driving as above average
topic: Why does almost everyone rate their own driving as above average?

name: Hindsight bias
mechanism: once you know how something turned out, it feels like you knew it all along, even if you had no way to predict it
example: this is why disasters always look obvious in hindsight after the fact
hook_subject: a surprising result feels obvious the moment you already know the outcome
topic: Why does a surprising result feel obvious the moment you already know the outcome?

name: Just-world hypothesis
mechanism: people assume the world is fundamentally fair, so they unconsciously blame victims for their own misfortune to preserve that belief
example: this is part of why people ask what a victim could have done differently
hook_subject: people blame victims to protect their belief that the world is fair
topic: Why do people blame victims just to protect their belief that the world is fair?

name: Fundamental attribution error
mechanism: we explain other people's mistakes as character flaws, but explain our own mistakes as caused by circumstances
example: if you're late it's traffic, if someone else is late they're careless
hook_subject: you blame the driver, not the traffic, when someone else cuts you off
topic: Why do you blame the driver, not the traffic, when someone else cuts you off?

name: Self-serving bias
mechanism: people credit their successes to their own skill, but blame their failures on bad luck or outside factors
example: a good grade is your talent, a bad grade is the test being unfair
hook_subject: you take credit for wins but blame luck for losses
topic: Why do you take credit for your wins but blame luck for your losses?

name: In-group bias
mechanism: we automatically trust and favor people who feel like they belong to our group, based on surprisingly shallow signals
example: this happens with something as trivial as wearing the same sports jersey
hook_subject: you trust a stranger faster just for liking the same team
topic: Why do you trust a stranger faster just for liking the same team?

name: Bandwagon effect
mechanism: believing something becomes easier the more other people around you already seem to believe it, independent of the evidence
example: this is why trending topics feel more true just for being popular
hook_subject: an idea feels more true just because it's trending
topic: Why does an idea feel more true just because it's trending?

name: Authority bias
mechanism: we assign more credibility to a claim simply because it comes from someone in a uniform, a title, or a position of authority
example: this is why a person in a lab coat is more persuasive, even off topic
hook_subject: a claim feels more true just because of who's saying it
topic: Why does a claim feel more true just because of who's saying it?

name: Primacy effect
mechanism: information presented first in a list or conversation is remembered better than what comes in the middle
example: first impressions stick harder than anything said afterward
hook_subject: the first thing someone tells you sticks harder than the rest
topic: Why does the first thing someone tells you stick harder than everything after it?

name: Recency effect
mechanism: the most recently presented information is remembered best, right after the primacy effect fades
example: this is why the last item in a list often gets picked most
hook_subject: the last thing said in a meeting often gets remembered best
topic: Why does the last thing said in a meeting often get remembered best?

name: Von Restorff effect
mechanism: an item that stands out from everything around it is remembered far better than the ones that blend in
example: this is why one red item on a shelf of gray ones gets picked first
hook_subject: the one different-looking option always grabs your attention first
topic: Why does the one different-looking option always grab your attention first?

name: Curse of knowledge
mechanism: once you understand something, it becomes hard to imagine what it's like not to know it, making you a worse teacher
example: experts often give confusing directions because they forgot what confusion feels like
hook_subject: experts give the worst directions because they forgot what confusion feels like
topic: Why do experts often give the worst directions, because they forgot what confusion feels like?

name: Illusory truth effect
mechanism: repeating a false statement enough times makes it feel true, purely from familiarity, not evidence
example: propaganda relies on repetition more than persuasion
hook_subject: a lie starts to feel true the more times you simply hear it
topic: Why does a lie start to feel true the more times you simply hear it?

name: Backfire effect
mechanism: being shown evidence that contradicts a belief can make some people cling to that belief even harder
example: fact-checking someone sometimes makes them more certain, not less
hook_subject: correcting someone's mistake sometimes makes them believe it more
topic: Why does correcting someone's mistake sometimes make them believe it even more?

name: Optimism bias
mechanism: most people believe they're less likely than average to experience bad outcomes, like divorce or job loss
example: this is part of why people underestimate their own risk in almost everything
hook_subject: you assume bad statistics apply to everyone except you
topic: Why do you assume bad statistics apply to everyone except you?

name: Planning fallacy
mechanism: people consistently underestimate how long a task will take, even when they've been wrong about the same thing before
example: this is why almost every renovation project runs over both budget and schedule
hook_subject: every project takes longer than you planned, even the ones you've done before
topic: Why does every project take longer than you planned, even ones you've done before?

name: Cognitive dissonance
mechanism: holding two conflicting beliefs creates real mental discomfort, which we resolve by quietly changing one of the beliefs, not our behavior
example: smokers who know the risks often downplay the statistics instead of quitting
hook_subject: you rewrite your own beliefs before admitting a decision was wrong
topic: Why do you rewrite your own beliefs before ever admitting a decision was wrong?

name: Effort justification
mechanism: the more painful or costly something was to obtain, the more we convince ourselves it was worth it
example: brutal fraternity hazing makes members value the group more, not less
hook_subject: you convince yourself something was worth it just because it was hard to get
topic: Why do you convince yourself something was worth it just because it was hard to get?

name: Psychological reactance
mechanism: being told you can't have or do something makes you want it more, purely because your freedom feels threatened
example: banning something is often the fastest way to make people want it
hook_subject: telling someone they can't have something makes them want it more
topic: Why does telling someone they can't have something make them want it more?

name: Gambler's fallacy
mechanism: believing that past random outcomes influence future ones, like assuming a coin is due for heads after several tails
example: roulette players bet heavily after a long losing streak for exactly this reason
hook_subject: you feel like a coin is due for heads after several tails, even though it isn't
topic: Why do you feel like a coin is due for heads after several tails, even though it isn't?

name: Hot-hand fallacy
mechanism: believing a streak of success makes more success more likely, even in situations that are actually random
example: basketball fans swear a player is on fire during a hot streak
hook_subject: you believe someone's on a hot streak, even when each shot is statistically independent
topic: Why do you believe someone's on a hot streak, even when each shot is independent?

name: Clustering illusion
mechanism: the human brain finds patterns in truly random data, because scattered randomness doesn't match our expectation of what random looks like
example: real random data always looks clumpier than people expect
hook_subject: random data always looks more clumped than real randomness should
topic: Why does random data always look more clumped than real randomness actually is?

name: Decoy effect
mechanism: adding a clearly worse third option changes which of the other two choices seems better, without changing either option itself
example: a medium popcorn priced near the large makes the large feel like a steal
hook_subject: a deliberately bad third option can make one of the other two look like a steal
topic: Why does a deliberately bad third option make one of the other two look like a steal?

name: Default effect
mechanism: people overwhelmingly stick with whatever option is pre-selected for them, even when changing it would take seconds
example: opt-out retirement plans get far more signups than opt-in ones
hook_subject: whatever option is pre-selected for you is the one you're most likely to keep
topic: Why does whatever option is pre-selected for you become the one you're most likely to keep?

name: Ambiguity aversion
mechanism: people prefer a known risk over an unknown one, even when the unknown option might statistically be better
example: people pick a familiar bad option over an unfamiliar uncertain one
hook_subject: you choose a known risk over an unknown one, even when the unknown one is better
topic: Why do you choose a known risk over an unknown one, even when the unknown one is better?

name: Present bias
mechanism: people consistently overvalue immediate rewards compared to larger rewards that are only slightly delayed
example: this is why saving for retirement feels so much harder than it should
hook_subject: a smaller reward right now can feel better than a bigger reward just a little later
topic: Why does a smaller reward right now feel better than a bigger reward just a little later?

name: Affect heuristic
mechanism: quick emotional reactions shape our judgment of risk and benefit before we've consciously reasoned anything out
example: things that feel scary get judged as more dangerous than the data supports
hook_subject: your gut feeling about something shapes your judgment before you've reasoned about it
topic: Why does your gut feeling shape your judgment before you've actually reasoned about anything?

name: Horn effect
mechanism: one negative trait about a person can unfairly taint how we judge every other unrelated trait about them
example: this is the mirror opposite of the halo effect, working just as fast
hook_subject: one bad trait can make someone seem worse at everything else too
topic: Why does one bad trait make someone seem worse at everything else too, unfairly?

name: Overjustification effect
mechanism: adding an external reward for something you already enjoyed doing can quietly kill your internal motivation to do it
example: kids who get paid to draw often draw less once the payments stop
hook_subject: paying someone for a hobby they already loved can make them enjoy it less
topic: Why does paying someone for a hobby they already loved make them enjoy it less?

name: Labeling effect
mechanism: giving someone a label, positive or negative, changes how they see themselves and often changes their actual behavior to match it
example: calling a kid the smart one can shape their identity for years
hook_subject: calling someone a label, even a kind one, can quietly shape who they become
topic: Why does calling someone a label, even a kind one, quietly shape who they become?

name: Self-fulfilling prophecy
mechanism: expecting a certain outcome can unconsciously change your behavior in ways that make that outcome more likely to happen
example: if you expect a meeting to go badly, you unconsciously behave in ways that make it go badly
hook_subject: expecting something to go badly can quietly make it go badly
topic: Why does expecting something to go badly quietly make it more likely to go badly?

name: Pygmalion effect
mechanism: when someone in authority expects more from you, they treat you differently in small ways that actually raise your performance
example: teachers told a class was gifted saw real, measurable score improvements
hook_subject: a teacher expecting more from you can actually raise your performance
topic: Why does a teacher simply expecting more from you actually raise your performance?

name: Stereotype threat
mechanism: reminding someone of a negative stereotype about their group right before a task can measurably hurt their performance on it
example: this happens even when the stereotype is one the person doesn't personally believe
hook_subject: being reminded of a stereotype about your group can hurt your performance
topic: Why does being reminded of a stereotype about your group hurt your performance on a task?

name: Illusion of transparency
mechanism: we consistently overestimate how obvious our own internal emotions are to the people watching us
example: your nervousness feels blazing obvious to you and almost invisible to everyone else
hook_subject: your nervousness feels obvious to you and almost invisible to everyone watching
topic: Why does your nervousness feel obvious to you and invisible to everyone watching?

name: False consensus effect
mechanism: people overestimate how much other people agree with their own opinions, habits, and choices
example: this is why everyone assumes their political views are the normal ones
hook_subject: you assume way more people agree with you than actually do
topic: Why do you assume way more people agree with you than actually do?

name: Diderot effect
mechanism: acquiring one new nice thing creates a craving to upgrade everything around it to match, spiraling into unplanned spending
example: a new couch suddenly makes the old rug and lamps look shabby by comparison
hook_subject: one new nice thing can make everything around it suddenly look shabby
topic: Why does one new nice thing make everything around it suddenly look shabby?

name: Streisand effect
mechanism: trying to hide or suppress information often draws far more attention to it than if it had just been ignored
example: this is named after an attempt to censor a photo that backfired spectacularly
hook_subject: trying to hide something can be exactly what makes everyone notice it
topic: Why does trying to hide something sometimes make everyone notice it even more?

name: Baader-Meinhof phenomenon
mechanism: after you first notice something, your brain starts spotting it everywhere, because it's now primed to look for it, not because it's more common
example: buy a certain car and suddenly you see that model everywhere
hook_subject: a word you just learned suddenly seems to show up everywhere afterward
topic: Why does a word you just learned suddenly seem to show up everywhere afterward?

name: Illusory superiority
mechanism: most people rate themselves as above average on nearly every desirable trait, which is mathematically impossible for most people
example: most people think they're more ethical, smarter, and more skilled than average
hook_subject: almost everyone secretly believes they're more ethical than average
topic: Why does almost everyone secretly believe they're more ethical than the average person?

name: Naive realism
mechanism: we assume our own perception of a situation is the objective truth, and anyone who disagrees must be biased, uninformed, or lying
example: two people can watch the same event and both feel certain the other is wrong
hook_subject: two people can watch the exact same event and both feel certain they saw the truth
topic: Why can two people watch the exact same event and both feel certain they saw the truth?

name: Actor-observer bias
mechanism: we explain our own actions by the situation, but explain other people's identical actions by their personality
example: you were stressed, they were just rude, for the exact same behavior
hook_subject: the exact same rude comment gets blamed on stress in you, and character in someone else
topic: Why does the exact same rude comment get blamed on stress in you, but character in someone else?

name: Egocentric bias
mechanism: we remember and recount past events in ways that quietly inflate our own role and contribution
example: in group projects almost everyone privately estimates they did more than their fair share
hook_subject: everyone on a team privately believes they did more than their fair share
topic: Why does everyone on a team privately believe they did more than their fair share?

name: Rosy retrospection
mechanism: past experiences are remembered as more pleasant than they actually felt while they were happening
example: the good old days always feel better in memory than they did in reality
hook_subject: the good old days always feel better in memory than they actually did
topic: Why do the good old days always feel better in memory than they actually did at the time?

name: Trait ascription bias
mechanism: we see ourselves as flexible and shaped by context, but see other people as having fixed, consistent personality traits
example: you think you're complicated, but assume everyone else is simply their type
hook_subject: you see yourself as complicated, but everyone else as simply their type
topic: Why do you see yourself as complicated, but everyone else as simply their type?

name: Social desirability bias
mechanism: people shade their answers on surveys and in conversation toward what sounds good, not what's actually true
example: self-reported exercise and income are notoriously inflated in surveys
hook_subject: people's self-reported habits are almost always a little more flattering than reality
topic: Why are people's self-reported habits almost always a little more flattering than reality?

name: Denomination effect
mechanism: the same amount of money feels easier to spend when it's in small bills or coins than when it's in one large bill
example: a pocket full of change disappears faster than a single big bill worth the same
hook_subject: loose change disappears faster than a big bill worth the exact same amount
topic: Why does loose change disappear faster than a big bill worth the exact same amount?

name: Mental accounting
mechanism: people treat money differently depending on which mental bucket it came from, even though all money is interchangeable
example: a tax refund gets spent freely in a way an equal amount of salary never would
hook_subject: a tax refund gets spent freely in a way the same amount of salary never would
topic: Why does a tax refund get spent freely in a way the same amount of salary never would?

name: Survivorship bias
mechanism: we judge success by studying only the people who made it, ignoring the much larger group who tried the same thing and failed
example: self-made success advice ignores everyone who did the same things and failed
hook_subject: success advice mostly comes from the few who made it, never the many who tried and failed
topic: Why does success advice mostly come from the few who made it, and never the many who tried?

name: Negativity bias
mechanism: the brain gives more weight and attention to negative information than to positive information of equal size
example: one bad review can outweigh fifty good ones sitting right next to it
hook_subject: one bad review can outweigh fifty good ones sitting right next to it
topic: Why does one bad review outweigh fifty good ones sitting right next to it?

name: Empathy gap
mechanism: we consistently underestimate how much our current emotional state will influence our future decisions
example: shopping hungry or deciding while angry both quietly warp your judgment more than expected
hook_subject: the emotional state you're in right now quietly warps decisions you think are rational
topic: Why does the emotional state you're in right now quietly warp decisions you think are purely rational?

name: Cheerleader effect
mechanism: individual faces are judged as more attractive when seen as part of a group than when seen alone
example: this is part of why group photos flatter people more than solo ones do
hook_subject: a face looks more attractive in a group photo than it does completely alone
topic: Why does a face look more attractive in a group photo than it does completely alone?

name: Priming effect
mechanism: exposure to one stimulus quietly changes how you respond to a related stimulus that comes right after it, without you noticing
example: reading words related to old age can measurably make people walk slower afterward
hook_subject: reading a few age-related words can make people walk slower minutes later
topic: Why does reading a few age-related words make people walk slower minutes later?

name: Door-in-the-face technique
mechanism: opening with a request so large it's guaranteed to be refused makes a smaller follow-up request far more likely to be accepted
example: asking for a huge favor first makes the real, smaller favor feel reasonable by comparison
hook_subject: a huge request that gets refused makes the smaller request right after it feel reasonable
topic: Why does a refused huge request make the smaller request right after it feel so reasonable?

name: Recognition heuristic
mechanism: when comparing two options, we assume the one we simply recognize is better, safer, or more important, purely from familiarity
example: a familiar brand name outsells a better but unknown product for this reason
hook_subject: a brand name you simply recognize can beat a better product you've never heard of
topic: Why does a brand name you simply recognize beat a better product you've never heard of?

name: Ostrich effect
mechanism: people actively avoid checking information that might be unpleasant, like a bank balance or a medical result, purely to avoid the discomfort
example: people delay opening bills they suspect are bad news for exactly this reason
hook_subject: avoiding a bank balance or a scale only delays the discomfort, it doesn't prevent it
topic: Why does avoiding a bank balance or a scale only delay the discomfort, not prevent it?

name: Groupthink
mechanism: the desire for harmony inside a group can override each member's better judgment, making everyone quietly agree to a plan nobody individually supports
example: this is part of how obviously bad decisions get approved unanimously in meetings
hook_subject: a group can unanimously agree to a plan that not one member actually supports
topic: Why does a group sometimes unanimously agree to a plan that nobody in it actually supports?
